reminder to self: 

some of the most successful founders I have seen on here have < 1000 followers 

ignore the vanity metrics 

keep building

This long weekend, X was a little slow. 

So I decided to use this as an opportunity to binge watch a bunch of starter story videos because I had nothing better to do 🙃 
 
I noticed a common theme among all of them, and that's when I realized those who are making a ton of money from their products all follow some of the same core principles.   

I did my best to synthesize the lessons from the ones that I watched.  Here is what I learned 👇

1. Sell before you build
Most founders build for months, then find out nobody wants it. 

Don't be that kind of founder who doesn't validate before building out a list of features. Make sure you use every single opportunity to put a "buy" button on your landing page. 
Maybe even put a real buy button online before the product is ready. Verbal interest really doesn't mean anything. Payment intent means everything.
Pre-sales tell you if you're building a painkiller or a vitamin.
2. Find ideas in pain you already know
The best ideas come from personal frustration or boring, overlooked industries. I was surprised about how many of these founders  build "boring" businesses. These markets have fewer competitors, stronger demand, and real buyers with urgent needs.
You don't always have to build something impressive, just need to build something people would actually pay for. 
3. Distribution is the moat
Building is easy now. Anyone can ship a product in a weekend.
Distribution is what separates the winners (subtle plug but I started a marketing/distribution newsletter called NewbieMarketer.to). 

Make sure you research the market. Search captures people already looking. Reddit gets you your first 100 customers. Creators drive strong conversions when they have skin in the game. 
4. Build fast. Build small.
Never spend more than 3 days  for MVPs. 

Break the app into blocks. 

Build one feature, one screen, one workflow at a time.
Do not rebuild what you have already built, reuse components. 
Speed beats perfection every time in the early stages. This has been said many times by Cal AI founder, Zach Yadegari many times as well. 
5. One core action wins
More features create more friction. 

Friction kills conversion and retention.
Find one specific painful workflow. Turn it into a simple automated tool. One clear use case is easier to sell than a broad platform.
Start narrow. Expand later.
6. Post relentlessly
Content creates demand before the product exists.
Post a lot to test hooks, angles, and messaging. Short-form platforms validate ideas fast. Three posts a day helps you find winning formats quickly.
The market will tell you which message resonates.
7. Run a portfolio of small bets
Don't bet everything on one idea.
Ship many products. Let the market decide what deserves more effort. Free side tools become acquisition channels. Related products protect you when one gets killed by a platform change or an algorithm update.
Build many. Double down on what works.
8. Action beats planning
The fastest way to learn is to build, launch, and get real feedback.
Don't wait until the idea feels perfect. Start with a small version and improve from real usage.
Momentum compounds. Planning doesn't.
9. Use the VSC framework to filter ideas
Not every idea is worth building. Run it through VSC first.
Virality: can it naturally spread? 
Scalability: can it grow without constant manual effort? 
Convertibility: are users actually likely to pay?
A good idea needs a believable path to attention, usage, and revenue. If it fails the VSC test, move on.
10. Speed is the solo founder's edge
With now AI disrupting how easy it is to build, you have toe build fast. Your advantage is urgency, fast shipping, and fast learning.
Keep showing up when the videos get 30 views. Keep building when the dashboard shows $0. Each failed product teaches you more than any book.
Launch before it feels ready.

Bonus: This video by Postiz Founder, @wickedguro,  is 10 minutes of pure gold:
 
Kudos to @thepatwalls for starting this because it's just a goldmine of lessons and if you have the time, you will really get a lot of value from watching a lot of these videos like I did. 

Thanks for reading, if you got this far!! :)
